abstract: This paper reviews and synthesizes the scholarly literature on the role of mainstream media in disseminating fake news. It highlights an apparent paradox: while fake news websites reach only small segments of the population, large proportions of the public are aware of and believe notable fake news stories. The authors argue this gap implies that mainstream media coverage of fake news may be a key vector through which such stories reach and influence the wider public, a role that has received limited scholarly attention.
key_claims: The direct reach of fake news websites is limited to relatively small parts of the population.
Despite this limited reach, large proportions of the public are aware of and believe notable fake news stories.
This discrepancy suggests most people encounter fake news through mainstream media coverage rather than through fake news websites directly.
The role of mainstream media in disseminating fake news has been understudied and deserves greater scholarly attention.
methods: Literature review and synthesis of existing research on fake news reach, awareness, belief, and mainstream media coverage.
findings: Empirical data show fake news websites attract limited audiences.
Survey and related data show widespread public awareness of and belief in prominent fake news stories.
The mismatch between limited website reach and broad public awareness points to mainstream media as a probable channel of dissemination.
contributions: Draws attention to the underexamined role of mainstream media in amplifying fake news.
Reframes the study of fake news dissemination to consider indirect pathways beyond fake news websites.
Provides a synthesis intended to guide future research on the causes and consequences of mainstream coverage of fake news.
framing: The paper situates itself within political communication and media studies scholarship on misinformation and fake news, extending the conversation from the reach of fake news sources toward the amplifying role of legacy mainstream news media.
